# Field Notes: The Intersection Nobody Fixes

Six accidents in four years at Maple and Ninth. Nobody died, thankfully, but two were bad enough for ambulances, and the city's own database (which took me three public-records requests to get) lists eleven more "near misses" logged by the traffic cameras since 2019. Eleven! And still no light, no four-way stop, nothing but a faded yield sign someone's pickup clipped last winter.

I went and stood there for an hour on a Tuesday, just watching. What you notice first is the sightline problem: a hedge on the northeast corner, maybe five feet tall, exactly tall enough to hide a sedan until it's already committed to the intersection. Someone trims that hedge maybe twice a summer. Nobody trims it enough.

The city's traffic engineer — I did eventually get her on the phone, after four voicemails — was not unsympathetic. She agreed the sightline was bad. She agreed the accident count justified a study. But a full signal warrant study costs around forty thousand dollars and takes, her words, "a year if we're lucky, two if we're not," and there are currently eleven intersections ahead of this one on the list. Eleven. The same number as the near misses, coincidentally, though that means nothing.

So what actually gets fixed first? Politics, mostly, though she wouldn't phrase it that way. Whichever council district makes noise. Whichever intersection has a school nearby, or a fatality, which is a grim kind of leverage nobody wants to use but everyone understands. Maple and Ninth has neither. It has a hardware store, a laundromat, and a lot of quiet residential traffic that never quite becomes a headline.

I don't have a tidy ending for this. The hedge is still there. The yield sign is still bent. Someone will get hurt badly enough, eventually, to move this up the list — that's how it tends to go, according to three separate people I talked to who've watched this exact pattern play out on other streets, in other years, with other hedges. It's a bad way to prioritize infrastructure. It's also, apparently, the only way that currently exists.
